In [[mathematics]], the '''Hopf lemma''', named after [[Eberhard Hopf]], states that if a [[continuous function|continuous]] [[real-valued function]] in a [[Domain (mathematical analysis)|domain]] in [[Euclidean space]] with sufficiently smooth boundary is [[Harmonic function|harmonic]] in the interior and the value of the function at a point on the boundary is greater than the values at nearby points inside the domain, then the [[directional derivative]] of the function in the direction of the outward pointing [[outer normal|normal]] is strictly positive. The lemma is an important tool in the proof of the [[maximum principle]] and in the theory of [[partial differential equation]]s. The Hopf lemma has been generalized to describe the behavior of the solution to an [[Elliptic partial differential equation|elliptic problem]] as it approaches a point on the boundary where its maximum is attained.

In the special case of the [[Laplacian]], the Hopf lemma had been discovered by [[Stanisław Zaremba (mathematician)|Stanisław Zaremba]] in 1910.<ref>M.S. Zaremba, Sur un problème mixte relatif à l’équation de Laplace, Bull. Intern. de l’Acad. Sci. de Cracovie, Ser. A, Sci. Math. (1910), 313–344.</ref> In the more general setting for elliptic equations, it was found independently by Hopf and [[Olga Oleinik]] in 1952, although Oleinik's work is not as widely known as Hopf's in Western countries.<ref>Hopf, Eberhard. A remark on linear elliptic differential equations of second order. Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. 3 (1952), 791–793.</ref><ref>Oleĭnik, O. A. On properties of solutions of certain boundary problems for equations of elliptic type. Mat. Sbornik N.S. 30 (1952), no. 72, 695–702.</ref> There are also extensions which allow domains with corners.<ref>Gidas, B.; Ni, Wei Ming; [[Louis Nirenberg|Nirenberg, L.]] Symmetry and related properties via the maximum principle. Comm. Math. Phys. 68 (1979), no. 3, 209–243.</ref>

==Statement for harmonic functions==
Let Ω be a bounded domain in '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup> with smooth boundary. Let ''f'' be a real-valued function continuous on the closure of Ω and [[harmonic function|harmonic]] on Ω. If ''x'' is a boundary point such that ''f''(''x'') > ''f''(''y'') for all ''y'' in Ω sufficiently close to ''x'', then the (one-sided) [[directional derivative]] of ''f'' in the direction of the outward pointing normal to the boundary at ''x'' is strictly positive.

==Proof for harmonic functions==
Subtracting a constant, it can be assumed that ''f''(''x'') = 0 and ''f'' is strictly negative at interior points near ''x''. Since the boundary of Ω is smooth there is a small ball contained in Ω the closure of which is tangent to the boundary at ''x'' and intersects the boundary only at ''x''. It is then sufficient to check the result with Ω  replaced by this ball. Scaling and translating, it is enough to check the result for the [[Unit sphere|unit ball]] in '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>, assuming ''f''(''x'') is zero for some unit vector ''x'' and ''f''(''y'') < 0 if |''y''| < 1.

By [[Harnack's inequality]] applied to −''f''

:<math>\displaystyle{-f(rx)\ge -{1-r\over (1+r)^{n-1}} f(0),}</math>

for ''r'' < 1. Hence

:<math>\displaystyle{{f(x)-f(rx)\over 1-r}={-f(rx)\over 1-r} \ge -{1\over (1+r)^{n-1}} f(0)> -{ f(0)\over 2^{n-1}} >0.}</math>

Hence the directional derivative at ''x'' is bounded below by the strictly positive constant on the right hand side.

==General discussion==
Consider  a second order, uniformly [[elliptic operator]] of the form
:<math> Lu = a_{ij}(x)\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x_i \partial x_j} + b_i(x) \frac{\partial u}{\partial x_i} + c(x)u, \qquad x \in \Omega.</math>
In particular, the smallest [[Eigenvalues and eigenvectors|eigenvalue]] of
the real [[symmetric matrix]] <math> a_{ij}(x) </math> is bounded from below by a positive constant that is independent of <math> x </math>.
Here <math>\Omega</math> is an open, bounded subset of <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math> and one assumes that <math> c \leq 0 </math>.

The Weak Maximum Principle states that a solution of the equation <math>Lu=0</math> in <math>\Omega</math> attains its maximum value on the closure <math>\overline{\Omega}</math> at some point on the boundary <math>\partial\Omega</math>.  Let <math>x_0 \in \partial\Omega</math> be such a point, then necessarily 
:<math> \frac{\partial u}{\partial \nu}(x_0) \geq 0,</math>
where <math>\partial/\partial\nu</math> denotes the outer normal derivative.  This is simply a consequence of the fact that <math>u(x)</math> must be nondecreasing as <math>x</math> approach <math>x_0</math>.  The Hopf lemma strengthens this observation by proving that, under mild assumptions on <math>\Omega</math> and <math>L</math>, we have

:<math> \frac{\partial u}{\partial \nu}(x_0) > 0.</math>

A precise statement of the Lemma is as follows.  Suppose that <math>\Omega</math> is a bounded region in <math>\mathbb{R}^2</math> and let <math>L</math> be the operator described above.  Let <math>u</math> be of class <math>C^2(\Omega) \cap C^1(\overline{\Omega})</math> and satisfy the differential inequality 
:<math> Lu \geq 0, \qquad \textrm{in}~ \Omega. </math>
Let <math>x_0 \in \partial\Omega</math> be given so that <math> 0\leq u(x_0) = \max_{x \in \overline{\Omega}} u(x)</math>.
If (i) <math>\Omega</math> is <math>C^2</math> at <math>x_0</math>, and (ii) <math>c \leq 0</math>, then either <math>u</math> is a constant, or <math> \frac{\partial u}{\partial \nu}(x_0) > 0</math>, where <math>\nu</math> is the outward pointing unit normal, as above.

The above result can be generalized in several respects.  The regularity assumption on <math>\Omega</math> can be replaced with an interior ball condition:  the lemma holds provided that there exists an open ball <math>B \subset \Omega</math> with <math>x_0 \in \partial B</math>.   It is also possible to consider functions <math>c</math> that take positive values, provided that <math>u(x_0) = 0</math>.  For the proof and other discussion, see the references below.{{Full citation needed|date=June 2025}}
